claims.text: A tailored post-processing heat treatment can induce uniformly distributed coherent nanoprecipitates in a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
Inducing coherent nanoprecipitates will enhance the alloy's radiation tolerance under fusion-relevant conditions.
A homogeneous tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy microstructure can be produced by additive manufacturing.
The additively manufactured initial alloy has a homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
The proposed radiation-tolerance benefit holds during helium-ion irradiation at approximately 900 °C and reactor-relevant fluences.
Coherent nanoprecipitates act as sinks for irradiation-induced point defects.
Coherent nanoprecipitates act as sinks for helium atoms.
Defect and helium trapping by the nanoprecipitates mitigates helium-bubble growth and coalescence.
Coherent precipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission.
Coherent nanoprecipitates can preserve high strength and tensile ductility in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys.
The heat-treated alloy will have a smaller average helium-bubble size than the unmodified alloy.
The heat-treated alloy will undergo less irradiation-induced hardening than the unmodified alloy.
The heat-treated alloy will preserve strength and ductility after helium irradiation.
Under equivalent irradiation, the unmodified alloy develops larger helium bubbles.
Under equivalent irradiation, the unmodified alloy experiences greater irradiation hardening.
The benefit may change at lower temperatures or under alternative irradiation regimes because nanoprecipitation kinetics or defect migration behavior changes.
The quantitative mechanical response may vary with processing details and irradiation dose.
The cited initial evidence supports defect annihilation by coherent nanoprecipitates.
